assessmentSummary.identity: One Short-Foot Drill repetition is performed on one target foot. Begin with the target heel, first metatarsal head, fifth metatarsal head, and relaxed long toes supported. Without curling or lifting the toes or rotating the ankle, draw the metatarsal heads toward the heel enough to shorten the foot and raise the medial arch, maintain the prescribed isometric hold, then relax with control to the same supported start. Record left and right separately. Standing hands-free, standing light wall-touch, and seated stable-bench support are exact variants. Hold time, comfortable submaximal effort and range, breathing, repetitions, sets, rest, side order, and delivery context are dosage or annotations. Toe Yoga, toe pressing or curling, whole-foot weight shifts, heel raises, dynamic-only contractions, single-leg or unstable support, maximal testing, biofeedback, and clinical treatment change the variant or definition.
currentCardFindings: Source 46 has a stable canonical identity and no direct name collision, but its definition and only variant are skeletal and do not supply a complete start, return endpoint, side-specific count, anatomy, loading, fatigue, delivery, substitution, persistence, or review contract.

The legacy description collapses standing and seated delivery into one ambiguous row and carries an age floor. The canonical version separates support variants and removes age and skill classification because exercise cards score the task only.

Direct doming research supports metatarsal-head-to-heel shortening, arch elevation, retained heel and forefoot contact, long toes, and rejection of toe curling, toe lifting, or ankle rotation. It does not establish a universal workout dose, outcome, recovery interval, or Vortex difficulty score.

Five YouTube candidates returned healthy oEmbed metadata. None has been watched in full, assigned to an exact support variant, or approved for mechanics, hold and return, count, captions, accessibility, cue quality, safety, or card-version match.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when the exact support variant, target side order, clean dry nonslip foot-safe surface, hygiene, toe visibility, comfortable submaximal arch shortening, symptoms, restrictions, hold dose, duration, and cumulative foot, toe, calf, balance, running, landing, jumping, agility, and lower-body budgets fit. Do not silently change support position, weight bearing, hand support, target side, toe action, contraction mode, assistance, resistance, count, clinical scope, or task identity. Recompute logistics, duration, fatigue, substitutions, persistence, and coach and athlete rendering after every change.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Direct doming strength-test mechanics, a randomized short-foot progression trial, an ultrasound-biofeedback motor-learning trial, a feasibility study documenting immediate learning difficulty, direct intrinsic-foot activation research, systematic reviews, general supervised-exercise safeguards, the exact Source 46 contract, five current YouTube oEmbed records, and comparison with Toe Yoga, tripod shifts, hallux pressing, toe flexion, single-leg balance, and short-foot-to-calf-raise neighbors
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: Research does not validate one universal support position, effort, range, hold, dose, frequency, fatigue ceiling, recovery interval, outcome, participant threshold, or Vortex score. Maximal strength testing and biofeedback research are not workout prescriptions. No media, relationship, or score has qualified human approval.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Place one target foot flat on a clean dry nonslip foot-safe surface with its heel, first metatarsal head, fifth metatarsal head, and relaxed long toes in contact. Without curling or lifting the toes or rotating the ankle, draw the metatarsal heads toward the heel enough to shorten the foot and raise the medial arch. Maintain the prescribed comfortable submaximal isometric hold, then relax with control to the same supported start. That dome, prescribed hold, and complete return on one target foot is one repetition. Record left- and right-foot repetitions and actual hold seconds separately. Standing hands-free, standing light wall-touch, and seated stable-bench support are explicit variants. Comfortable submaximal range and effort, hold duration, breathing, repetitions, sets, rest, side order, foot covering, and delivery context are annotations. Simultaneous feet, toe extension or flexion, hallux pressing, whole-foot weight shifts, dynamic-only or eccentric-only action, manual assistance, resistance, biofeedback, unstable or single-leg support, heel raise, maximal assessment, or clinical treatment require a separately reviewed variant or definition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of doming and toe flexion testing to quantify foot muscle strength
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Doming draws the metatarsal heads toward the heel while raising the arch and retaining foot contact.
Vortex defines one target-foot dome, prescribed hold, and controlled return as one repetition; support variants and side-specific counting are explicit.

evidence.sourceTitle: Randomized Clinical Trial: The Effect of Exercise of the Intrinsic Muscle on Foot Pronation
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Short-foot exercise is an arch-shortening task distinct from selective toe extension and whole-foot pressure shifting.
Seated, loaded seated, standing, and single-leg conditions change support or loading and are not silently collapsed.

evidence.sourceTitle: Intrinsic Foot Muscle Activation During Specific Exercises: A T2 Time Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
claims: Short-foot exercise activated all measured plantar intrinsic foot muscles in the study.
The card includes intrinsic and extrinsic contributors, joints, actions, planes, contacts, and laterality without claiming isolation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of doming and toe flexion testing to quantify foot muscle strength
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Valid doming keeps the toes and heel down while the forefoot draws toward the heel; toe or heel lifting invalidated trials.
Workout repetitions additionally require no toe curl, no ankle rotation, a submaximal hold, and a controlled return.

evidence.sourceTitle: Relationship of Physical Factors to the Acceptability and Unacceptability of Short Foot Exercise: A Preliminary Study
claims: Short-foot exercise was technically challenging and many participants could not perform it acceptably even after practice.
Candidate scores describe task complexity and physical difficulty only, not participant proficiency, eligibility, or age.

evidence.sourceTitle: Intrinsic Foot Muscle Activation During Specific Exercises: A T2 Time Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
claims: Short-foot exercise produced measurable plantar intrinsic activation in an acute laboratory protocol.
Laboratory exposure does not establish workout fatigue or recovery; Vortex tracks repetitions, hold seconds, support, faults, symptoms, and overlapping foot load.

evidence.sourceTitle: Relationship of Physical Factors to the Acceptability and Unacceptability of Short Foot Exercise: A Preliminary Study
claims: The feasibility protocol used seated support, first-metatarsal-head and heel contact, arch elevation, and rejected interphalangeal flexion or ankle rotation.
Vortex adds surface, hygiene, visibility, wall, bench, symptom, communication, space, and exit constraints without demographic classification.

evidence.sourceTitle: Randomized Clinical Trial: The Effect of Exercise of the Intrinsic Muscle on Foot Pronation
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Published protocols vary and the trial authors did not identify one universal short-foot protocol.
Candidate hold and repetition ranges remain quarantined and stop before contact, long-toe, arch, ankle, body, breathing, or symptom quality degrades.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of doming and toe flexion testing to quantify foot muscle strength
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: A direct instruction is to draw the ball of the foot toward the heel and raise the arch without curling or lifting the toes.
Vortex adds target side, submaximal hold, controlled relaxation, valid count, support position, and stop rules.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: General exercise safeguards emphasize qualified instruction, safe environments, appropriate progression, and technique supervision.
No age or participant level is inferred; exact-task control, symptoms, environment, exposure, and facility escalation govern selection.

evidence.sourceTitle: Evidence for Intrinsic Foot Muscle Training in Improving Foot Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
claims: Intrinsic-foot programs are heterogeneous in exercise selection, dose, and outcomes.
Short-Foot Drill may serve preparation or resilience only when purpose and fatigue budgets fit; no universal outcome is promised.

evidence.sourceTitle: Relationship of Physical Factors to the Acceptability and Unacceptability of Short Foot Exercise: A Preliminary Study
claims: Acceptable performance can require practice and is defined by observable contacts and absence of toe flexion and ankle rotation.
Athlete support uses small comfortable doming, long toes, quiet contacts, full relaxation, breathing, and symptom checks rather than maximal effort.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of doming and toe flexion testing to quantify foot muscle strength
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Toe, first-metatarsal-base, and heel lifting were observable invalid-trial criteria.
Coaches record support, side, contacts, toe curl or lift, ankle rotation, arch action, return, first fault, exposure, symptoms, and duration without diagnosing impairment.

evidence.sourceTitle: Randomized Clinical Trial: The Effect of Exercise of the Intrinsic Muscle on Foot Pronation
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Seated support preceded progressively loaded and standing practice in one protocol.

Seated support, visible cue cards, smaller effort, shorter holds, fewer repetitions, more rest, captions, transcript, stills, or live instruction may improve access; assistance is a separate candidate variant.

evidence.sourceTitle: How to Evaluate and Improve Foot Strength in Athletes: An Update
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: Short-foot, selective toe extension, toe-spread, and toe-flexion exercises have different action contracts.
Support variants, modifiers, single-leg, unstable, assisted, resisted, dynamic-only, maximal-test, biofeedback, and compound boundaries remain explicit.
